newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Longtime Nicaraguan foes sign electoral pact.
newsitem.headline: Longtime Nicaraguan foes sign electoral pact.

text.p: Amid shouting protesters, a faction of Nicaragua's former Contra rebels on Wednesday signed an election pact with the left-wing Sandinista Front against whom they fought a bloody civil war in the 1980s.

Calling the alliance an act of national reconciliation, former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega embraced many of the right-wing rebels who had tried to topple his 1979-1990 government in a war that left 30,000 dead.

"On this historic date, we have signed this crucial alliance to reunite the Nicaraguan family, guarantee peace and fight poverty," Ortega said amid jeering from a group of hardline Contras opposed to the alliance.
The Sandinistas and U.S.-backed Contras fought an eight-year civil war that ended in 1990 after President Violeta Chamorro's surprise election victory over Ortega.
The government promised the Contras land and credit if they demobilized, promises that went largely unfulfilled.
After the war the 22,000 Contras splintered into many factions, ending their chances of becoming a major political force.

"We'll never forget what happened during the war, but a time comes when the country needs peace and reconciliation," former Contra commander Denis Galeano, who had four family members killed during the war, told Reuters.

Galeano, known as Commander Johnny during the war, said many former Contras live in poverty and that he signed the pact because the Sandinistas were the only party to offer them a political space to pursue their demands.

Sandinista officials said the alliance would bring 4,500 demobilized Contras to the Sandinistas, who are running a close second to right-wing candidate Arnoldo Aleman in Nicaragua's Oct. 20 presidential elections.
In exchange for their support, the Sandinistas promised the ex-Contras three ministries if they won the election.
The pact was part of a Sandinista strategy to leave their radical left-wing roots behind and include diverse segments of Nicaraguan society on their election platform.
But most former Contras did not join the alliance, including their official political body, the Nicaraguan Resistance Party.
"I don't see it as a sign of political reconciliation, but as a show with political ends," former Contra commander Luis Fley told Reuters.
